candidate.answerReason: The four games have two possible outcomes each, giving 16 histories. The prize order reconstructs all four game results, so these histories give 16 distinct prize orders.

methods.label: Count the four game outcomes
methods.explanation:
There are four games, and each has two possible winners. Although earlier winners determine the participants in later games, there are still exactly two choices at every step. The multiplication principle therefore gives
\[
2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2=16
\]
possible sequences of game results.

We must check that these sequences give different prize orders. A prize order tells us the loser of every game: the fifth-, fourth-, and third-prize recipients lose the first three games, and the second-prize recipient loses the final game. Starting with bowlers #5 and #4, these losers determine each successive survivor and hence reconstruct all four game results. Thus two different result sequences cannot give the same prize order.

Every legal prize order comes from a sequence of game results, so the count is exactly \(16\), choice B.
methods.levelReason: Four successive binary choices and an elementary reconstruction argument establish the count.
